# CANDIDATE-001: OpenSSH resets its receive sequence number on a stray NEWKEYS under strict KEX

Status: **candidate**, confirmed by replay on OpenSSH 9.2p1 (Debian) and 10.6p2 (Alpine edge, current), root cause located in upstream source; maintainers not contacted.
Published on 2026-11-07 by team decision: we assess it as a spec ambiguity that an on-path attacker cannot trigger (see below).

## Observation

Target: OpenSSH 9.2p1 from Debian bookworm (`targets/openssh`, strict KEX backport), client offers `kex-strict-c-v00@openssh.com`.
After a completed handshake, the client sends SSH_MSG_NEWKEYS outside any key exchange
(pre-auth, after a refused rekey, or post-auth).
The server answers SSH_MSG_UNIMPLEMENTED, keeps the current keys,
and resets its receive sequence number to 0.

Evidence (`scripts/seqnr_experiment.py`, 3 runs each, deterministic):

| Variant | Next packet |
|---|---|
| A: strict KEX, client keeps its sequence number | MAC failure, connection closed |
| B: no strict KEX | accepted |
| C: strict KEX, client resets its own sequence number to 0 | accepted |

Dropbear 2024.85 and AsyncSSH 2.17.0 disconnect on the same stray NEWKEYS.
First noticed by the Codex mapper agent from server debug output while fixing a mapper bug,
then confirmed by Claude with the experiment above.

## Root cause

Upstream `openssh-portable` master, `packet.c`, in the receive path (`ssh_packet_read_poll2`, lines 1860–1863 when read on 2026-11-07):

```c
if (*typep == SSH2_MSG_NEWKEYS && ssh->kex->kex_strict) {
    debug_f("resetting read seqnr %u", state->p_read.seqnr);
    state->p_read.seqnr = 0;
}
```

The reset happens in the packet layer for every received NEWKEYS,
before the dispatcher decides the message is unexpected and answers UNIMPLEMENTED,
so the counter is reset although no new keys are installed.
The send path (lines 1380–1383) has the same shape, but OpenSSH only sends NEWKEYS inside a key exchange.

## Why it matters (assessment, low confidence)

draft-miller-sshm-strict-kex-01 §3.3 / OpenSSH PROTOCOL §1.9: the sequence number is reset after sending or receiving NEWKEYS.
The text does not say whether this applies to a NEWKEYS that is not part of a key exchange.
OpenSSH follows the literal text; the other two treat the message as a protocol error.
This looks like a **spec ambiguity** rather than a vulnerability:
only a party holding the session keys can send an encrypted NEWKEYS, so an on-path attacker cannot trigger it.
With `chacha20-poly1305@openssh.com` (nonce = sequence number), a reset without rekeying would reuse nonces
for the sending client's own later packets, if the client also reset; we have not tested other ciphers.

## Next checks

1. ~~Current upstream OpenSSH~~: same behaviour in 10.6p2.
2. ~~Read upstream `packet.c`~~: done, see Root cause.
3. Other strict-KEX implementations (Go x/crypto/ssh, libssh, russh, wolfSSH, MINA): does any other reset without new keys?
4. Test with `chacha20-poly1305@openssh.com` once the mapper supports it.
5. Decide with the team whether this is worth a note to the OpenSSH developers and to the draft author.
"""Does a server reset its receive sequence number on a NEWKEYS that is not part of a key exchange?

Variants after a completed handshake, for each target:
  A  strict KEX on,  client keeps its sequence number after the stray NEWKEYS
  B  strict KEX off, client keeps its sequence number
  C  strict KEX on,  client resets its own outgoing sequence number to 0 after the stray NEWKEYS
If A fails, B succeeds and C succeeds, the server reset its receive counter without new keys.
"""
from smlearn import testbed
from smlearn.ssh.mapper import SSHMapper

WORDS = {
    "pre-auth refused rekey": (["KEXINIT", "KEX30", "NEWKEYS", "SR_AUTH", "KEXINIT", "KEX30", "NEWKEYS"], "UA_PW_OK"),
    "pre-auth bare NEWKEYS": (["KEXINIT", "KEX30", "NEWKEYS", "SR_AUTH", "NEWKEYS"], "UA_PW_OK"),
    "post-auth bare NEWKEYS": (["KEXINIT", "KEX30", "NEWKEYS", "SR_AUTH", "UA_PW_OK", "NEWKEYS"], "CH_OPEN"),
}

import sys
for name in (sys.argv[1:] or ["openssh", "dropbear", "asyncssh"]):
    inst = testbed.start(testbed.load_target(name))
    try:
        for label, (prefix, probe) in WORDS.items():
            row = []
            for variant, strict, reset in (("A", True, False), ("B", False, False), ("C", True, True)):
                m = SSHMapper(inst.host, inst.port, timeout=0.4, quiet=0.1, strict_kex=strict)
                outs = set()
                for _ in range(3):
                    m.reset()
                    pre = [m.step(i) for i in prefix]
                    if reset:
                        m.outgoing.sequence = 0
                    outs.add((pre[-1], m.step(probe)))
                m.close()
                (last, probe_out), = outs if len(outs) == 1 else [("NONDET", str(outs))]
                row.append(f"{variant}: NEWKEYS->{last}, {probe}->{probe_out}")
            print(f"{name:9} {label:24} | " + " | ".join(row))
    finally:
        inst.stop()
# SSH mapper specification

The mapper turns abstract input symbols into concrete SSH transport messages,
sends them to a real server,
and turns everything the server sends back into one abstract output symbol.
The learning algorithm only ever sees abstract symbols,
so the mapper must be **deterministic**:
the same input sequence after `reset()` must always give the same outputs.

It lives in `src/smlearn/ssh/` and is implemented from the RFCs only
(RFC 4251–4254, RFC 8731, RFC 5656, RFC 4344, RFC 6668,
and OpenSSH `PROTOCOL` section 1.9 at V_9_6_P1 and draft-miller-sshm-strict-kex-01 for strict KEX).
**No third-party SSH library** (no paramiko, asyncssh, etc.):
use `cryptography` for X25519, AES-CTR and HMAC.

## Interface

```python
from smlearn.ssh.mapper import SSHMapper, INPUTS

m = SSHMapper(host, port, user="test", password="test", strict_kex=True)
m.reset()                  # new TCP connection, version exchange, absorb server KEXINIT
out = m.step("KEXINIT")    # -> "KEXINIT" etc.
m.trace                    # list of (direction, msg_name, payload_hex) for the current query
m.close()
```

Constructor keyword arguments, with defaults:
`timeout=1.0` (max seconds to wait for the first reply packet in a step),
`quiet=0.15` (after a packet arrives, keep reading until nothing arrives for this long),
`strict_kex=True` (advertise `kex-strict-c-v00@openssh.com`).

`reset()` closes any previous connection,
opens a new one,
sends `SSH-2.0-smlearn_0.1\r\n`,
reads the server identification line (skipping any lines before it that do not start with `SSH-`),
and absorbs whatever the server sends during the quiet window,
which is normally its KEXINIT.
The server KEXINIT payload is stored for the exchange hash.
Nothing received during `reset()` is reported as output.

## Algorithms

Offer exactly one algorithm per category, so negotiation is deterministic:

- kex: `curve25519-sha256` (plus `kex-strict-c-v00@openssh.com` when `strict_kex=True`)
- host key: `ssh-ed25519,rsa-sha2-256,ecdsa-sha2-nistp256` (the signature is not verified; this is a local testbed)
- cipher: `aes128-ctr`
- MAC: `hmac-sha2-256`
- compression: `none`

## Input alphabet

`INPUTS` is this tuple, in this order:

| Symbol | Concrete message |
|---|---|
| `KEXINIT` | SSH_MSG_KEXINIT (20) with a fixed cookie of 16 zero bytes |
| `KEX30` | SSH_MSG_KEX_ECDH_INIT (30) with a fresh X25519 public key |
| `NEWKEYS` | SSH_MSG_NEWKEYS (21) |
| `SR_AUTH` | SSH_MSG_SERVICE_REQUEST (5) for `ssh-userauth` |
| `SR_CONN` | SSH_MSG_SERVICE_REQUEST (5) for `ssh-connection` |
| `UA_PW_OK` | SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_REQUEST (50), method `password`, correct credentials |
| `UA_PW_NOK` | same with a wrong password |
| `UA_NONE` | SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_REQUEST (50), method `none` |
| `CH_OPEN` | SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_OPEN (90), type `session`, window 2^21, max packet 32768 |
| `CH_CLOSE` | SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_CLOSE (97) |
| `CH_EOF` | SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_EOF (96) |
| `CH_DATA` | SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_DATA (94) with data `b"x"` |
| `CH_REQUEST_EXEC` | SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_REQUEST (98) `exec`, want_reply true, command `true` |
| `IGNORE` | SSH_MSG_IGNORE (2) with empty data |
| `DEBUG` | SSH_MSG_DEBUG (4), always_display false, empty message and language |
| `UNIMPLEMENTED` | SSH_MSG_UNIMPLEMENTED (3) with sequence number 0 |
| `DISCONNECT` | SSH_MSG_DISCONNECT (1), reason 11 (BY_APPLICATION) |

### Mapper state and out-of-order inputs

Inputs can arrive in any order.
The mapper must send them anyway whenever it can build the bytes,
because how the server reacts to unexpected messages is exactly what we want to learn.

- The mapper keeps the latest client KEXINIT payload it sent,
  the latest server KEXINIT payload it received,
  and its latest X25519 private key.
- When a KEX_ECDH_REPLY (31) arrives,
  and the mapper has both KEXINIT payloads and a private key,
  it computes the shared secret, the exchange hash H and the session id
  (H of the first exchange, never replaced on rekey),
  and derives *pending* keys (RFC 4253 section 7.2).
  If it is missing something, it derives nothing.
- Pending keys are kept **per direction** and are consumed when installed:
  each key exchange that completes (a KEX_ECDH_REPLY processed as above) gives one pending key set for outgoing
  and one for incoming.
- Sending `NEWKEYS` switches the **outgoing** direction to its pending keys, if there are any, and clears them;
  otherwise the outgoing direction keeps its current keys, cipher state and sequence number unchanged.
- Receiving NEWKEYS from the server switches the **incoming** direction to its pending keys, if there are any, and clears them;
  otherwise the incoming direction is unchanged.
  (Re-installing already used keys would restart the AES-CTR keystream, and the peer would see a MAC failure that is
  an artifact of the mapper, not behaviour of the server.)
- Strict KEX applies when the mapper offered it and the server's KEXINIT contained `kex-strict-s-v00@openssh.com`.
  Then the outgoing sequence number resets to 0 when sending NEWKEYS installs new keys,
  and the incoming one resets to 0 when receiving NEWKEYS installs new keys.
- Sequence numbers count every packet in each direction from the start of the connection (uint32, wrapping).
- The channel inputs `CH_CLOSE`, `CH_EOF`, `CH_DATA` and `CH_REQUEST_EXEC` use the server's channel id
  from the latest CHANNEL_OPEN_CONFIRMATION.
  If no channel is open, the mapper sends nothing and the output is `NO_CHANNEL`.
  `CH_OPEN` is always sent.
  After the mapper sends or receives CHANNEL_CLOSE, the channel is no longer open.
- The mapper never answers server messages on its own:
  no automatic replies to KEXINIT, GLOBAL_REQUEST, CHANNEL_REQUEST or window adjustments.

## Output abstraction

`step()` sends the message, then reads packets:
it waits up to `timeout` for the first one,
and after each packet keeps reading until nothing arrives for `quiet` seconds.
The output is the names of the received messages joined with `+`, in arrival order.

Message names: `DISCONNECT, IGNORE, UNIMPLEMENTED, DEBUG, SERVICE_ACCEPT, EXT_INFO, KEXINIT, NEWKEYS, KEX31, UA_FAILURE, UA_SUCCESS, UA_BANNER, GLOBAL_REQUEST, REQUEST_SUCCESS, REQUEST_FAILURE, CH_OPEN_SUCCESS, CH_OPEN_FAILURE, CH_WINDOW_ADJUST, CH_DATA, CH_EXTENDED_DATA, CH_EOF, CH_CLOSE, CH_REQUEST, CH_SUCCESS, CH_FAILURE`.
Any other message number becomes `MSG<n>`.
Consecutive repeats of the same name collapse into one (for example `CH_DATA+CH_DATA` becomes `CH_DATA`),
because their number depends on timing.

Special outputs:

- `NO_RESP`: nothing arrived within `timeout`.
- `+CLOSED`: appended when the connection closes (EOF or reset) during the step, e.g. `DISCONNECT+CLOSED`, or just `CLOSED` when nothing came before it.
- `NO_CONN`: the connection was already closed before this step. Nothing is sent.
- `NO_CHANNEL`: see above.
- `BAD_PACKET`: an incoming packet could not be decrypted or failed its MAC check.
  The mapper then treats the connection as closed.

`trace` is reset by `reset()` and records every packet sent and received in the current query,
as `(">" or "<", name, payload.hex())`,
so any disagreement can be replayed and inspected.

## Validation

The tests in `tests/test_ssh_mapper.py` run against real servers in Docker
(OpenSSH, Dropbear, AsyncSSH)
and must all pass:
the happy-path handshake completes,
wrong credentials fail,
repeated queries give identical outputs,
and closed connections behave as specified.

After `reset()`, `strict_kex_active` is `True` when strict KEX applies to this connection (see above), else `False`.

# CANDIDATE-001 verification

Verified on 2026-11-07 by source inspection and experiments against Docker targets bound to 127.0.0.1.
Verdict: **confirmed** for the server after initial KEX, with important client-state and impact qualifications.
No downloaded source was built or executed.
The only existing repository file read for execution was the authorized experiment; this report is a new file.

## 1. Receive path and key state — confirmed

In [V_10_6_P1 packet.c:1736–1786](https://github.com/openssh/openssh-portable/blob/V_10_6_P1/packet.c#L1736), the packet is authenticated/decrypted using the current receive sequence number, that original number is saved for dispatch, and the counter is incremented.
At packet.c:1849–1852, the test is simply "'`if (*typep == SSH2_MSG_NEWKEYS && ssh->kex->kex_strict)`, followed by `state->p_read.seqnr = 0;`.
It does not test whether a KEX is active or new keys are pending.
This occurs inside `ssh_packet_read_poll2()` before it returns through the read API to the dispatcher.
In [V_10_6_P1 dispatch.c:87–114](https://github.com/openssh/openssh-portable/blob/V_10_6_P1/dispatch.c#L87), reading precedes `(*ssh->dispatch[type])(type, seqnr, ssh)`.
Thus the reset precedes the decision that NEWKEYS is unexpected.
The UNIMPLEMENTED payload contains the original received sequence number, not the reset value.

In [V_10_6_P1 kex.c:429–437](https://github.com/openssh/openssh-portable/blob/V_10_6_P1/kex.c#L429), `kex_send_newkeys()` resets the transport dispatch table, sends NEWKEYS, then registers `kex_input_newkeys` as the expected receive handler.
At kex.c:562–575, the legitimate receive handler immediately restores NEWKEYS to `kex_protocol_error`, checks the payload end, and calls `ssh_set_newkeys(ssh, MODE_IN)`.
At kex.c:600–603 it marks KEX complete and clears `KEX_INITIAL` and KEX-init flags.
At kex.c:994–1015, strict KEX is selected only during initial KEX by checking the opposite role'"'s strict marker, and remains enabled afterwards.
At kex.c:232–246, "'`kex_protocol_error()` disconnects for an unexpected message during strict initial KEX, but otherwise constructs `SSH2_MSG_UNIMPLEMENTED` and returns success.

The exact handler outside KEX depends on the application phase, rather than always being `dispatch_protocol_error()`.
[V_10_6_P1 auth2.c:175–179](https://github.com/openssh/openssh-portable/blob/V_10_6_P1/auth2.c#L175) initializes the server authentication dispatcher with `dispatch_protocol_error`.
[V_10_6_P1 serverloop.c:905–922](https://github.com/openssh/openssh-portable/blob/V_10_6_P1/serverloop.c#L905) does the same for the server connection loop and explicitly enables KEXINIT for rekeying.
Both that default handler, at dispatch.c:40–51, and `kex_protocol_error()` send UNIMPLEMENTED.
Neither installs keys.

[V_10_6_P1 packet.c:976–1040](https://github.com/openssh/openssh-portable/blob/V_10_6_P1/packet.c#L976) shows that installing keys requires moving `ssh->kex->newkeys[mode]` into packet state and rebuilding the cipher context via `cipher_init()`.
The stray-message receive branch never calls this routine.
The receive key, cipher context, CTR/CBC state or GCM invocation state, and MAC key stay in use; only the SSH receive sequence counter is reset by this branch.
The opposite direction'"'s send counter is not reset by receiving NEWKEYS, including when sending the UNIMPLEMENTED response.
The send-side reset at packet.c:1376–1382 is adjacent to an unconditional "'`ssh_set_newkeys(ssh, MODE_OUT)` for an outgoing NEWKEYS, so it must not be described as an equivalent supported way for OpenSSH to send stray NEWKEYS while retaining keys.

## 2. OpenSSH client symmetry — partly

The packet-layer behavior is shared between client and server and the receive reset has no role check.
After authentication, [V_10_6_P1 clientloop.c:2844–2862](https://github.com/openssh/openssh-portable/blob/V_10_6_P1/clientloop.c#L2844) sets the default handler to `dispatch_protocol_error`, enables KEXINIT, and leaves stray NEWKEYS on the default error path.
An established client therefore also resets, sends UNIMPLEMENTED, retains current keys, and continues.
After a subsequent completed KEX, the restored `kex_protocol_error` handler has the same nonfatal outcome.

During user authentication, however, [V_10_6_P1 sshconnect2.c:462–465 and 563–566](https://github.com/openssh/openssh-portable/blob/V_10_6_P1/sshconnect2.c#L462) installs `input_userauth_error` as the default handler, which calls `fatal_f("bad message during authentication: type %d", type)`.
In that phase a stray server NEWKEYS still resets the counter first, but terminates the client instead of sending UNIMPLEMENTED and continuing.
Unexpected initial strict-KEX NEWKEYS also terminates through KEX error handling.
Client conclusions are source-verified, not reproduced with a malicious local server.

## 4. Protocol impact — partly; misbehaving peer required

A party creating a fresh valid encrypted NEWKEYS after initial KEX needs the relevant directional encryption and authentication keys, barring cryptographic compromise or forgery.
This can be the legitimate remote endpoint and does not require successful SSH user authentication.
A passive observer or ordinary on-path attacker cannot choose or modify an authenticated packet'"'s type to trigger this reset.
An attacker can retransmit ciphertext, so “only key holders can send one” needs the qualification that creation of a fresh valid packet differs from replay.
With two honest endpoints, old NEWKEYS packets do not provide this trigger: initial NEWKEYS was under the initial unencrypted transport, and rekey NEWKEYS was protected with the preceding keys, which the receiver replaces upon legitimate processing.
The finding supplies no way for an on-path attacker to get a valid stray NEWKEYS under the receiver's current keys and sequence state between honest endpoints.

For "'`chacha20-poly1305@openssh.com`, [V_10_6_P1 cipher-chachapoly.c:77–110 and 125–134](https://github.com/openssh/openssh-portable/blob/V_10_6_P1/cipher-chachapoly.c#L77) derives the nonce and per-packet Poly1305 key from `POKE_U64(seqbuf, seqnr)`.
After a misbehaving peer supplies the stray message, the honest receiver reuses old receive-side key/nonce combinations when processing sequence numbers starting again at zero.
Previously recorded packets from that same direction and current key epoch can then authenticate and decrypt again at matching sequence numbers, subject to application-state validation and intervening rekeying or closure.
A peer which also resets its sending counter and encrypts new packets under the retained key causes actual encryption nonce and Poly1305-key reuse in its own sending direction.
